evidence.title: Manila Port Authority — Manifest Discrepancy Notice
evidence.content: Container MNL-KHH-03 appears on two separate bills of lading, both filed within the same shipping cycle, both referencing prefix COR-1978. Physically, a container cannot be in two places on one manifest cycle.

evidence.title: Bill of Lading — Entry A (Manila)
evidence.content: Declared cargo: industrial fittings. Consignee: a Manila-registered trading office. Reference: COR-1978-M.

evidence.title: Bill of Lading — Entry B (Kaohsiung transshipment)
evidence.content: Declared cargo: identical fittings, identical weight, different declared value. Consignee: a Kaohsiung-registered forwarding office. Reference: COR-1978-K.

evidence.title: Corvid Systems — Corporate Filing
evidence.content: Both consignee offices resolve to subsidiaries of one parent: Corvid Systems, self-described as a "global resilience & risk consulting" firm. This is the first filing that connects the shell used in Case 001 and the mirroring node used in Case 002 to one named company.

chat.text: Three cases in, and Manila's just handed me a container that's apparently in two places on paper. I think we've been looking at pieces of one thing.

cctv.name: Manila Terminal Gate 3
cctv.normalText: GATE 3 — ROUTINE. Container MNL-KHH-03 logged departing on schedule.
cctv.clueText:
[NO PHYSICAL RE-ENTRY]

Gate log confirms the container left Manila once and never returned. The Kaohsiung entry is a paperwork duplicate, not a second physical container.

archive.title: Bill of Lading — COR-1978-M
archive.commentary: Filed by the Manila-registered trading office. Declared value is roughly 40% lower than the Kaohsiung entry for identical cargo.

archive.title: Bill of Lading — COR-1978-K
archive.summary: Kaohsiung-declared transshipment entry for the same container.
archive.commentary: Filed by the Kaohsiung forwarding office on the same cycle. The value gap between the two entries is the actual crime — laundering cargo value through a paper duplicate, not moving anything twice.

archive.title: Corvid Systems — Registered Subsidiaries
archive.summary: Corporate filing listing both the Manila and Kaohsiung consignee offices as subsidiaries of Corvid Systems.
archive.commentary: First document tying both offices, and by extension both prior cases' shells, to one named parent company.

map.name: MNL-KHH-03
map.notes: Declared route only — the physical container never left Manila's terminal twice.

puzzles.successOutput:

2 records matched prefix COR-19.
Both resolve to subsidiaries of a single parent entity.

Single physical container. Two declared routes. One is a paperwork ghost.
See Map for physical vs. declared overlay.

suspects.name: Corvid Systems — Manila/Kaohsiung Shipping Subsidiary
suspects.notes: No individual filed either bill of lading personally — the entity itself is the culprit. First organizational suspect entry in the campaign.

solution.successMessage: There's no person to arrest here — the duplicate manifest is a mechanism, and the mechanism belongs to Corvid Systems. Flagging the subsidiary is the only submission that fits what the evidence actually shows.

onDocument.c3_ev04: Corvid Systems. Not a shell this time — a real company, with a real name, sitting behind two shells from two different cases.

onFlag.ARCHIVE_TRACED: Same fingerprints, third country. This isn't three cases anymore.

onBookmark.c3_ev04: Bookmarked. Corvid Systems — full name confirmed.

narrativeBeats.onSubmitSuccess: Submission flags the subsidiary. Regulators are notified. Renata's gone quiet on the line — she's already thinking about what comes next.
